A chronological prefix does not create a genuine holdout if the frozen SASRec already trained on its target interaction. Removing that target from inference inputs cannot remove information learned in the weights; perturbation results remain descriptive training-example sensitivity, not evidence of generalization or improvement from retraining. Sequential-recommendation studies also identify cross-user temporal leakage: per-user chronological splits can still expose globally future interactions. [Data-leakage study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060), [sequential splitting study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16289).

Recommended construction, inferred from these findings: split only the prescribed training histories before fitting separate diagnostic models. Reserve chronological suffixes, train from fresh initialization on earlier prefixes, and evaluate each target using only its preceding history. Exclude reserved suffixes from training inputs, positive targets, and interaction-derived statistics. Use a common timestamp cutoff when claiming globally future prediction. For cross-fitting, each scored target needs a model fitted without that target or later information; ordinary random folds do not enforce chronology. Fine-tuning the contaminated checkpoint does not establish exclusion. These auxiliary experiments leave the official benchmark splits and evaluator unchanged. [Cross-fitting construction](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12658738/).

Predictive validity requires another separation: define diagnostic metrics and their predicted intervention gains on development variants, then freeze that rule before evaluating previously unseen model variants. Compare predictions against measured changes in the prescribed macro validation HR@10, using paired candidates/users; report rank correlation, gain-sign accuracy, and uncertainty. Input-perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish that an architecture or training change will help. Treat this as a proposed validation design, not an established SASRec result; repeated adaptation to the same validation scores introduces selection bias. [Model-selection overfitting](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
